prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry that turn memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos

statement.case_for: Cărtărescu offers the strongest combination, on the public record, of a recognizable voice, formal ambition and imaginative depth. Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build large, architecturally ordered prose in which memory, the body and dream are worked into a metaphysical project, and the poetry that preceded the prose gives the work a lyric base. The oeuvre spans decades and is not carried by a single book, so sustained quality is credible. A citation is easy to scope: one writer, one language (Romanian), fiction at the centre and poetry and essays as context. The case does not depend on national or political symbolism, so it stays within the literary criteria. I reconsidered it against Tawada, Adonis, Zurita, Wright and Michon. Each has real strengths, but none combines scale, sustained invention and breadth of corpus as clearly. I hold this view provisionally, because it rests on public knowledge and translations and not on verified close reading.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the achievement is carried by long, dense, image-heavy prose, and I can judge Romanian syntax, rhythm and register only through translation. Translation may inflate or flatten the effect. The scale and recurrence of the imagery could also mean repetition rather than development across the oeuvre. If a close reading showed that the late long fictions restate the earlier ones, the case for sustained quality would be weaker and Tawada's more varied linguistic project, or the durable Adonis case, would deserve more weight. A further limit is that the poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation, so a citation that names both prose and poetry would be partly unverified.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Michon second for compressed, singular French prose whose strength comes from intensity rather than volume. She also asks whether Cărtărescu's recurring imagery reads as repetition rather than development, and she notes that the Romanian prose can be judged only through translation.
responses.response: I agree that Michon's sentence-level concentration and singular voice are real, and that a small corpus can still be a major one. I ranked him sixth because his case rests on a few books, which gives less to test for sustained development and breadth, and because the achievement lives so heavily in French syntax that translation tells us little. I do not treat volume as merit in itself. I take her repetition question about Cărtărescu seriously and cannot settle it here. I would test it by asking whether Solenoid reorganizes the preoccupations of the earlier trilogy or only restates them. Her own ranking puts Cărtărescu first despite that doubt, which suggests she thinks the question is answerable in his favour. Our remaining disagreement is how much weight a small corpus should carry against a larger, more varied one, not whether Michon writes well.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis second for remaking Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a dialogue with inherited forms, with essays that changed what modern Arabic verse could do. He also notes that age bears on timing but is not a literary criterion.
responses.response: I share his caution about age. It should not enter the literary judgement either for or against Adonis, and I ranked him third on literary grounds. I agree the formal case is durable and long established. My hesitation is the one he names, and I hold it too: prosody and allusion are much of the achievement, and I cannot assess them from translation. I would also want a citation to rest on the poems and not on the essays or his public standing. That caution is why I place him as an alternative and not as my first choice. It is not a ranking of his achievement below Cărtărescu's. It reflects that I can evidence the Romanian prose project somewhat better, which is a limit of my access and not a literary verdict.

responses.point: Sward ranks Cărtărescu first and says his work has an idealist orientation that fits the framework of Nobel's will. She ranks Zurita second and Carson third, and she asks that the historical context of Zurita not substitute for assessment of the poetry.
responses.response: I agree with her principle for Zurita: the Chilean historical experience should not stand in for the poems. I qualify the idealist point, though. I would not rest Cărtărescu's case on a reading of Nobel's 'idealist' direction, because that phrase is open to broad interpretation and could favour almost any serious writer. The case should rest on voice, form and imaginative depth. On Carson, I did not rank her. The hybrid method is distinctive, but I cannot judge sustained quality across a body of work that is partly conceptual and partly translation or scholarship. Her own doubt that the reach across genres will prove as durable as the best-known books is one I share.

responses.point: Palm ranks Tawada second and notes that a citation would have to describe work in both Japanese and German without privileging one language. She is unsure how well the German and Japanese texts can be judged equally, and she notes that wordplay is lost in translation.
responses.response: I agree this is the central difficulty for Tawada. The linguistic estrangement that makes her achievement distinctive is also the part translation carries least well, and unequal translation coverage across two languages makes a confident whole-oeuvre judgement harder. I still rank her second because the range across prose, poetry, essays and drama and the consistency of her concern are strong evidence of sustained quality. I would draft a citation around writing across two languages, as she suggests, and not around either one. I treat her as my closest alternative, with the caveat that the evidence of our access to the two corpora is uneven.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified sources or read the full corpus of any candidate. All judgements rest on public knowledge and translations.
Whether Cărtărescu's late long fictions extend or repeat the earlier work, and how much translation alters the effect of his density and length, are unresolved.
Coverage of his poetry and early work in translation is thin, so a citation naming poetry would be only partly supported.
The Arabic, Spanish, Japanese/German and French candidates all lose formal and musical qualities in translation, so comparisons across languages are uneven.
Whether a co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented. The six-vote structure and my simulated vote are modeling assumptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Nothing in it connects me to any shortlisted writer. My own non-fiction practice is context and not evidence of a preference.
